claim: The extracellular matrix (ECM) protein laminin-111 (LN1) plays an indispensable role in the formation of normal breast acini.
source: Previously, we documented both the indispensable role of the extracellular matrix (ECM) protein, laminin-111 (LN1), in the formation of normal breast acini, and the phenotypic reversion of cancer cells to acini-like structures in 3-dimensional (3D) gels with inhibitors of oncogenic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as a previously documented finding in the abstract, referencing prior work by the authors.

claim: Cancer cells can undergo phenotypic reversion to acini-like structures in 3D gels when treated with inhibitors of oncogenic pathways.
source: Previously, we documented both the indispensable role of the extracellular matrix (ECM) protein, laminin-111 (LN1), in the formation of normal breast acini, and the phenotypic reversion of cancer cells to acini-like structures in 3-dimensional (3D) gels with inhibitors of oncogenic pathways.
evidence: This is stated as a previously documented finding in the abstract.

claim: A reciprocal circuitry comprising laminin-5 (LN5), nitric oxide (NO), p53, HOXD10 and three microRNAs is involved in the formation of mammary acini in 3D.
source: We report a surprising reciprocal circuitry comprising positive players: laminin-5 (LN5), nitric oxide (NO), p53, HOXD10 and three microRNAs (miRNAs) — that are involved in the formation of mammary acini in 3D.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on the experimental work described in the manuscript.

claim: Cancer cells on 2D or 3D and non-malignant cells on 2D plastic do not produce NO.
source: Significantly, cancer cells on either 2-dimensional (2D) or 3D and non-malignant cells on 2D plastic do not produce NO and upregulate negative players: NFκB, EIF5A2, SCA1 and MMP-9 — that disrupt the network.
evidence: This is stated as a significant finding in the abstract, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Cancer cells on 2D or 3D and non-malignant cells on 2D plastic upregulate NFκB, EIF5A2, SCA1 and MMP-9.
source: Significantly, cancer cells on either 2-dimensional (2D) or 3D and non-malignant cells on 2D plastic do not produce NO and upregulate negative players: NFκB, EIF5A2, SCA1 and MMP-9 — that disrupt the network.
evidence: This is stated as a significant finding in the abstract, supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Introducing exogenous NO to cancer cells reintegrates signaling pathways and induces phenotypic reversion in 3D.
source: Introducing exogenous NO, LN5 or individual miRNAs to cancer cells reintegrates these pathways and induces phenotypic reversion in 3D.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental interventions described in the manuscript.

claim: Introducing exogenous LN5 to cancer cells reintegrates signaling pathways and induces phenotypic reversion in 3D.
source: Introducing exogenous NO, LN5 or individual miRNAs to cancer cells reintegrates these pathways and induces phenotypic reversion in 3D.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental interventions described in the manuscript.

claim: Introducing individual miRNAs to cancer cells reintegrates signaling pathways and induces phenotypic reversion in 3D.
source: Introducing exogenous NO, LN5 or individual miRNAs to cancer cells reintegrates these pathways and induces phenotypic reversion in 3D.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract based on experimental interventions described in the manuscript.

claim: The balance between positive and negative players leads to homeostasis in breast epithelial architecture.
source: These findings uncover the essential elements of breast epithelial architecture, where the balance between positive- and negative-players leads to homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: p53 is aberrant in almost all cancer types.
source: p53 is an extensively characterized regulator of gene expression in the context of malignant transformation and is aberrant in almost all cancer types.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Many p53 studies have been performed in cells cultured in 2D conditions.
source: Many p53 studies have been performed in cells cultured in 2D conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about the existing literature in the introduction.

claim: Little is known about what regulates p53 activity in higher organisms in vivo.
source: Despite the extensive literature on p53 and its myriad of functions, little is known about what regulates p53 activity in higher organisms in vivo or about how p53 might regulate physiological tissue functions in 3D cultures (Barcellos-Hoff et al., 1989; Petersen et al., 1992; Bissell et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Little is known about how p53 might regulate physiological tissue functions in 3D cultures.
source: Despite the extensive literature on p53 and its myriad of functions, little is known about what regulates p53 activity in higher organisms in vivo or about how p53 might regulate physiological tissue functions in 3D cultures (Barcellos-Hoff et al., 1989; Petersen et al., 1992; Bissell et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated as a gap in knowledge in the introduction, with citations to support the claim.

claim: ECM proteins, in particular laminins, play a role in glandular tissue morphogenesis.
source: ECM proteins, in particular LNs (Miner and Yurchenco, 2004), compose another important class of regulators that play a role in glandular tissue morphogenesis.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The HMT3522 cancer progression series comprises primary normal epithelial cells (S1) derived from reduction mammoplasty.
source: This unique series comprise both primary normal epithelial cells or non-malignant cells (S1) derived from reduction mammoplasty, and their malignant counterpart (T4-2), which were derived without external oncogenic agents after prolonged cultivation in defined medium that lacked epidermal growth factor (EGF), followed by xenografts in animals (Briand et al., 1987).
evidence: This describes the cell line series used in the study, with a citation to the original source.

claim: The HMT3522 cancer progression series comprises malignant cells (T4-2) derived without external oncogenic agents after prolonged cultivation in defined medium that lacked EGF, followed by xenografts in animals.
source: This unique series comprise both primary normal epithelial cells or non-malignant cells (S1) derived from reduction mammoplasty, and their malignant counterpart (T4-2), which were derived without external oncogenic agents after prolonged cultivation in defined medium that lacked epidermal growth factor (EGF), followed by xenografts in animals (Briand et al., 1987).
evidence: This describes the cell line series used in the study, with a citation to the original source.

claim: Non-malignant mammary cells form polarized colonies resembling normal acini of the breast in 3D LN1-rich ECM gels.
source: Non-malignant mammary cells form polarized colonies resembling normal acini of the breast (Barcellos-Hoff et al., 1989), whereas malignant cells form disorganized, tumor-like structures (Petersen et al., 1992; Lee et al., 2007; Rizki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic of the cell lines, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Malignant cells form disorganized, tumor-like structures in 3D LN1-rich ECM gels.
source: Non-malignant mammary cells form polarized colonies resembling normal acini of the breast (Barcellos-Hoff et al., 1989), whereas malignant cells form disorganized, tumor-like structures (Petersen et al., 1992; Lee et al., 2007; Rizki et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as an established characteristic of the cell lines, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Downmodulating receptors such as integrins and EGFR, or other involved oncogenic pathways to a level found in normal cells, causes every single malignant cell to form polarized growth-arrested colonies through a process called phenotypic reversion.
source: However, if the architecture of colonies is restored in LN1 gels by downmodulating receptors such as integrins and EGFR, or other involved oncogenic pathways to a level found in normal cells, every single malignant cell would form polarized growth-arrested colonies – by a process we call phenotypic reversion – through a novel movement we have termed 'coherent angular motion' (CAMo) (Tanner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Phenotypic reversion occurs through a novel movement termed 'coherent angular motion' (CAMo).
source: However, if the architecture of colonies is restored in LN1 gels by downmodulating receptors such as integrins and EGFR, or other involved oncogenic pathways to a level found in normal cells, every single malignant cell would form polarized growth-arrested colonies – by a process we call phenotypic reversion – through a novel movement we have termed 'coherent angular motion' (CAMo) (Tanner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A subset of 60 genes had similar expression patterns in S1 and in all of the T4-2 Rev cells.
source: Using S1 cells, T4-2 cells and T4-2 cells reverted to 'normal' phenotype (T4-2 Rev) by five different signaling inhibitors, we identified a subset of 60 genes that had similar expression patterns in S1 and in all of the T4-2 Rev cells (Bissell et al., 2005; Becker-Weimann et al., 2013), as well as 10 miRNAs that could potentially target these 60 genes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with citations to support the claim.

claim: 10 miRNAs could potentially target the 60 genes identified in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells.
source: Using S1 cells, T4-2 cells and T4-2 cells reverted to 'normal' phenotype (T4-2 Rev) by five different signaling inhibitors, we identified a subset of 60 genes that had similar expression patterns in S1 and in all of the T4-2 Rev cells (Bissell et al., 2005; Becker-Weimann et al., 2013), as well as 10 miRNAs that could potentially target these 60 genes.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with citations to support the claim.

claim: miR-34c-5p, miR-30e, and miR-144 are dramatically downmodulated in many breast tumors.
source: Among the 10 miRNAs, we specifically focused on miR-34c-5p, −30e, and −144, which are dramatically downmodulated in many breast tumors (Lu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the literature, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Restoration of miR-34c-5p, miR-30e, or miR-144 caused phenotypic reversion of T4-2 cells in lrECM.
source: Restoration of the miRNA caused phenotypic reversion of T4-2 cells in lrECM.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: A reciprocal regulatory network comprising LN1 and LN5, NO, p53, HOXD10, NFκB, the three miRNAs, EIF5A2, SCA1, and MMP-9 connects the ECM-laminins and the nuclear transcription factors to execute breast morphogenetic programs.
source: While studying the signaling cascades that involve these three miRNAs, we identified a reciprocal regulatory network – comprising LN1 and LN5, NO, p53, HOXD10, NFκB, the three miRNAs, EIF5A2, SCA1, and MMP-9 – which connects the ECM-laminins and the nuclear transcription factors (TFs), most possibly via a newly discovered nuclear tunnel (Jorgens et al., 2017), to execute breast morphogenetic programs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with a citation to a related work.

claim: The reciprocal regulatory network may connect ECM-laminins and nuclear transcription factors via a newly discovered nuclear tunnel.
source: While studying the signaling cascades that involve these three miRNAs, we identified a reciprocal regulatory network – comprising LN1 and LN5, NO, p53, HOXD10, NFκB, the three miRNAs, EIF5A2, SCA1, and MMP-9 – which connects the ECM-laminins and the nuclear transcription factors (TFs), most possibly via a newly discovered nuclear tunnel (Jorgens et al., 2017), to execute breast morphogenetic programs.
evidence: This is stated as a speculative finding from the study, with a citation to a related work.

claim: Inhibitory antibodies to beta-1 integrin reverted malignant T4-2 cells to 'normal' phenotype.
source: We showed initially that inhibitory antibodies to beta-1 integrin reverted the malignant cells to 'normal' phenotype (Figure 1a) (Weaver et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with a citation and reference to Figure 1a.

claim: Inhibiting EGFR, PI3K, or MMP-9 could revert breast cancer cells.
source: Inhibiting any of a dozen different oncogenic pathway components, including EGFR, PI3K and MMP-9, could revert breast cancer cells (Figure 1a–1c) (Bissell et al., 2005; Beliveau et al., 2010; Becker-Weimann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with citations and reference to Figure 1a-1c.

claim: Array analyses of the five most prominent reverting pathways identified 60 genes that were low in S1, and co-downregulated in T4-2 Rev cells.
source: Array analyses of the five most prominent reverting pathways identified 60 genes that were low in S1, and co-downregulated in T4-2 Rev cells (Figure 1d, Table 1) (Bissell et al., 2005), leading us to suspect that the common regulators would be miRNAs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with a citation and reference to Figure 1d and Table 1.

claim: miRNA expression profiling of S1, T4-2, and T4-2 Rev cells in lrECM identified a list of 30 miRNAs, the expression of which was anti-correlated with that of the 60 genes.
source: miRNA expression profiling of the S1, T4-2, and T4-2 Rev cells in lrECM identified a list of 30 miRNAs, the expression of which was anti-correlated with that of the 60 genes (Figure 1d, Table 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 1d and Table 2.

claim: 10 validated miRNAs were chosen that could potentially target at least 10 out of the 60 genes.
source: By combining these two lists, we chose 10 validated miRNAs (Figure 2a) each of which could potentially target at least 10 out of the 60 genes (Table 3).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 2a and Table 3.

claim: miR-34c-5p, miR-30e, and miR-144 were significantly reduced in breast tumors compared to normal tissues.
source: By in situ hybridization of tissue arrays containing 40 breast tumors vs. normal tissues, we confirmed a significant reduction of the three miRNAs in tumors (Figure 2b, c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 2b and 2c.

claim: Re-expression of each of the three miRNAs in T4-2 cells led to dramatic growth inhibition in soft agar.
source: Re-expression of each of the three miRNAs in T4-2 cells led to dramatic growth inhibition in soft agar (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) and caused phenotypic reversion in lrECM (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 2d and Figure 2—figure supplement 1b.

claim: Re-expression of each of the three miRNAs in T4-2 cells caused phenotypic reversion in lrECM.
source: Re-expression of each of the three miRNAs in T4-2 cells led to dramatic growth inhibition in soft agar (Figure 2d, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b) and caused phenotypic reversion in lrECM (Figure 2e, Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Introduction of each of the three miRNAs into metastatic MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells led to severe growth impairment in lrECM.
source: Introduction of each of the three miRNAs into metastatic MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells also led to severe growth impairment in lrECM (Figure 2f, Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 2f and Figure 2—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The three miRNAs are involved in inhibiting tumor cell growth and in the maintenance of non-malignant cell behavior.
source: These results suggest that the three miRNAs are involved in inhibiting tumor cell growth and, by implication, in the maintenance of non-malignant cell behavior.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: EIF5A2 and SCA1 are the only common target genes of the three miRNAs among the 60 genes that were modulated by each of five reverting agents.
source: A search of the miRNA target database (microRNA.org) identified EIF5A2 and SCA1 as the only common target genes of the three miRNAs among the 60 genes that were modulated by each of five reverting agents (Table 4, Figure 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Table 4 and Figure 1.

claim: Endogenous levels of EIF5A2 and SCA1 were high in T4-2 cells compared to those in S1 cells.
source: Endogenous levels of the two proteins were high in T4-2 cells compared to those in S1 cells, but as expected, were downmodulated in T4-2 Rev cells that were reverted either with a reverting agent or upon restoration of any of the three miRNAs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: EIF5A2 and SCA1 were downmodulated in T4-2 Rev cells that were reverted either with a reverting agent or upon restoration of any of the three miRNAs.
source: Endogenous levels of the two proteins were high in T4-2 cells compared to those in S1 cells, but as expected, were downmodulated in T4-2 Rev cells that were reverted either with a reverting agent or upon restoration of any of the three miRNAs (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: Depletion of either EIF5A2 or SCA1 in T4-2 cells with shRNA caused phenotypic reversion.
source: Importantly, depletion of either EIF5A2 or SCA1 in T4-2 cells with shRNA (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a) also caused phenotypic reversion (Figure 3b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1a and 1b.

claim: Restoration of EIF5A2 or SCA1 severely impaired tumor-cell reversion.
source: Restoration of EIF5A2 or SCA1 severely impaired tumor-cell reversion, validating the importance of the inactivation of these two target genes for normal functional differentiation of breast acini (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 3—figure supplement 1d and 1e.

claim: The activity of the 1–0 kb region for miR-34c promoter was high in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, but not in T4-2 cells.
source: The activity of the 1–0 kb region for miR-34c and the 3–0 kb region for both miR-30e and −144 was high in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, but not in T4-2 cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 3c.

claim: The activity of the 3–0 kb region for both miR-30e and miR-144 promoters was high in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, but not in T4-2 cells.
source: The activity of the 1–0 kb region for miR-34c and the 3–0 kb region for both miR-30e and −144 was high in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, but not in T4-2 cells (Figure 3c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 3c.

claim: Multiple high-confidence binding sites for HOXD10 and NFκB were identified in the critical regions of the miRNA promoters.
source: To determine which TFs bound to these critical regions, we analyzed the PROMO database (Farré et al., 2003) and identified multiple high-confidence binding sites for HOXD10 and NFκB (% dissimilarity <15%; genomic frequency <1×10−4) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a, Table 6) (Farré et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1a and Table 6, and a citation to the PROMO database.

claim: Overexpression of HOXD10 phenotypically reverts T4-2 cells.
source: We had shown previously that overexpression of HOXD10 or downmodulation of NFκB phenotypically reverts T4-2 cells (Becker-Weimann et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Downmodulation of NFκB phenotypically reverts T4-2 cells.
source: We had shown previously that overexpression of HOXD10 or downmodulation of NFκB phenotypically reverts T4-2 cells (Becker-Weimann et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with citations to support the claim.

claim: HOXD10 was high in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells compared to T4-2 cells.
source: As predicted, HOXD10 was high in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells compared to T4-2 cells (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4a.

claim: Activation of NFκB, as measured by Ser536 phosphorylation of the p65 subunit, was elevated in T4-2 cells and downmodulated in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells.
source: By contrast, activation of NFκB, as measured by Ser536 phosphorylation of the p65 subunit that causes its nuclear translocation (Sasaki et al., 2005), was elevated in T4-2 cells and downmodulated in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4a and a citation to support the method.

claim: Depletion of p65 or p50 in T4-2 cells elevated the activity of the miRNA promoters.
source: In all these conditions, the activity of the miRNA promoters was elevated in the same regions as those described above (Figure 4b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Overexpression of HOXD10 in T4-2 cells elevated the activity of the miRNA promoters.
source: In all these conditions, the activity of the miRNA promoters was elevated in the same regions as those described above (Figure 4b, Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Depletion of p65 or p50 in T4-2 cells increased miRNA expression and allowed the formation of basally polarized colonies in lrECM.
source: Northern analysis confirmed the increase of miRNA expression, allowing the formation of basally polarized colonies in lrECM (Figure 4c and d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), which were analogous to colonies of miRNAs-expressing T4-2 cells (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4c, 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, and Figure 2c.

claim: Overexpression of HOXD10 in T4-2 cells increased miRNA expression and allowed the formation of basally polarized colonies in lrECM.
source: Northern analysis confirmed the increase of miRNA expression, allowing the formation of basally polarized colonies in lrECM (Figure 4c and d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c), which were analogous to colonies of miRNAs-expressing T4-2 cells (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4c, 4d, Figure 4—figure supplement 1c, and Figure 2c.

claim: HOXD10 bound the promoters of the three miRNAs in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, but not in T4-2 cells.
source: We found that HOXD10 bound the promoters of the three miRNAs in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, but not in T4-2 cells, whereas the NFκB p65 subunit bound the same regions in T4-2 cells, but not in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: The NFκB p65 subunit bound the promoters of the three miRNAs in T4-2 cells, but not in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells.
source: We found that HOXD10 bound the promoters of the three miRNAs in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, but not in T4-2 cells, whereas the NFκB p65 subunit bound the same regions in T4-2 cells, but not in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells (Figure 4e, Figure 4—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4e and Figure 4—figure supplement 1d.

claim: Expression of wild-type NFκB decoys, but not mutant decoys, derepressed the promoter activities in T4-2 cells.
source: The expression of wild-type NFκB decoys, but not mutant decoys, derepressed the promoter activities, showing that the wild-type decoys bound and sequestered NFκB, whereas the mutant decoys did not.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Expression of wild-type HOXD10 decoys, but not mutant decoys, inhibited the promoter activities in HOXD10-overexpressing T4-2 cells.
source: The procedure was repeated for HOXD10 with similar conclusions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 4—figure supplement 1e.

claim: HOXD10 and NFκB directly bind specific sequences in miRNA promoters in a mutually exclusive manner to regulate miRNA expression for restoration of breast acinar architecture.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that HOXD10 and NFκB directly bind the specific sequences in miRNA promoters in a mutually exclusive manner to regulate miRNA expression for restoration of breast acinar architecture.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Appreciable levels of wild-type p53 were found in the epithelial compartment of sections of normal breast tissues but not in the stroma.
source: We found appreciable levels of wild-type p53 in the epithelial compartment of sections of normal breast tissues but not in the stroma (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: Appreciable levels of Ser20-phosphorylated p53 (pSer20-p53) were found in 3D cultures of S1 and T4-2 Rev cells.
source: In 3D cultures of S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, we found appreciable levels of Ser20-phosphorylated p53 (pSer20-p53), which stabilizes (Chehab et al., 1999) and enhances the transactivation activity of p53 (Jabbur et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with citations to support the functional significance of the phosphorylation.

claim: Ser20 phosphorylation of p53 stabilizes p53.
source: In 3D cultures of S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, we found appreciable levels of Ser20-phosphorylated p53 (pSer20-p53), which stabilizes (Chehab et al., 1999) and enhances the transactivation activity of p53 (Jabbur et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Ser20 phosphorylation of p53 enhances the transactivation activity of p53.
source: In 3D cultures of S1 and T4-2 Rev cells, we found appreciable levels of Ser20-phosphorylated p53 (pSer20-p53), which stabilizes (Chehab et al., 1999) and enhances the transactivation activity of p53 (Jabbur et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The expression of the p53-regulated genes, p21, GADD45 and DRAM, was elevated in S1 and all T4-2 Rev cells.
source: The expression of the p53-regulated genes, p21, GADD45 and DRAM, was elevated in S1 and all T4-2 Rev cells (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: Expression of DNp53 prevented S1 cells from forming polarized quiescent acini in lrECM.
source: As expected, expression of DNp53 prevented S1 cells from forming polarized quiescent acini in lrECM (Figure 5c, Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 5c and Figure 5—figure supplement 1a.

claim: RNAi-mediated depletion of wild-type p53 in S1 or MCF10A cells abrogated acinar formation.
source: Similarly, RNAi-mediated depletion of the wild-type p53 in S1 or MCF10A cells abrogated acinar formation (Figure 5d and e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 5d, 5e, Figure 5—figure supplement 1b and 1c.

claim: Inhibition of p53 activity with α-pifithrin rendered T4-2 cells resistant to phenotypic reversion by any of the reverting agents tested.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of p53 activity with a specific inhibitor, α-pifithrin (Komarov et al., 1999), rendered T4-2 cells resistant to phenotypic reversion by any of the reverting agents tested (Bissell et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2007, 2012) or by re-expression of any of the three miRNAs (Figure 5f and g, Figure 5—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 5f, 5g, Figure 5—figure supplement 1d and 1e, and citations to support the reverting agents.

claim: Inhibition of p53 activity with α-pifithrin rendered T4-2 cells resistant to phenotypic reversion by re-expression of any of the three miRNAs.
source: Furthermore, inhibition of p53 activity with a specific inhibitor, α-pifithrin (Komarov et al., 1999), rendered T4-2 cells resistant to phenotypic reversion by any of the reverting agents tested (Bissell et al., 2005; Lee et al., 2007, 2012) or by re-expression of any of the three miRNAs (Figure 5f and g, Figure 5—figure supplement 1d and e).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 5f, 5g, Figure 5—figure supplement 1d and 1e, and citations to support the reverting agents.

claim: MCF10A cells that overexpressed DNp53 were resistant to reverting agents.
source: Likewise, MCF10A cells that overexpressed DNp53, were resistant to reverting agents (Figure 5h, Figure 5—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 5h and Figure 5—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Formation of acini and production of milk proteins required an endogenously formed basement membrane even after placing cells in lrECM.
source: We had shown previously that even after placing cells in lrECM, formation of acini and production of milk proteins still required an endogenously formed BM (Streuli and Bissell, 1990).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: A significant increase in human laminins was observed in both conditioned media and lysates of S1 and T4-2 Rev cells reverted by expression of miRNAs or depletion of the two target genes.
source: Using a human-specific pan-LN antibody, we observed a significant increase in human LNs in both CM and lysates of S1 and T4-2 Rev cells reverted by expression of miRNAs or depletion of the two target genes (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1a.

claim: The α3, β3 and γ2 chains of LN5 were highly elevated in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells that expressed the miRNAs or that were depleted of their two targets.
source: The α3, β3 and γ2 chains of LN5 were highly elevated in S1 and T4-2 Rev cells that expressed the miRNAs or that were depleted of their two targets.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Parental T4-2 cells did not produce LN5.
source: By contrast, parental T4-2 cells did not produce LN5, suggesting that LN5 is only expressed in MECs capable of forming acinar-like polarized structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b–d).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1b-d.

claim: Loss of LAMA3 abrogated reversion of T4-2 cells with any of the different reverting agents including any of the three miRNAs.
source: Loss of LAMA3 abrogated reversion of T4-2 cells with any of the different reverting agents including any of the three miRNAs (Figure 6a and b, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a, b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 6a, 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a and 2b.

claim: Depletion of LAMA3 could be rescued by addition of ectopic LN5.
source: Depletion of LAMA3 could be rescued by addition of ectopic LN5, confirming the specificity of the reaction (Figure 6a and b, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a and b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 6a, 6b, Figure 6—figure supplement 2a and 2b.

claim: MMP-9 was significantly reduced in T4-2 cells that expressed any of the three miRNAs or were depleted of the two target genes, EIF5A2 and SCA1.
source: We measured the level of secreted MMP-9 in lrECM cultures and showed that MMP-9 was significantly reduced in T4-2 cells that expressed any of the three miRNAs- or were depleted of the two target genes, EIF5A2 and SCA1 (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 6c.

claim: Both EIF5A2 and SCA1 lie downstream of the PI3K/AKT pathway and are involved in positive regulation of MMP transcription.
source: It had been shown previously that both EIF5A2 and SCA1 lie downstream of the PI3K/AKT pathway and are involved in positive regulation of MMP transcription (Liu et al., 2000; Park et al., 2013; Khosravi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Expression of the miRNAs inactivates both EIF5A2 and SCA1 and thus downmodulates MMP-9 leading to stabilization of LN5.
source: We concluded that expression of the miRNAs inactivates both EIF5A2 and SCA1 and thus downmodulates MMP-9 leading to stabilization of LN5.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Laminin was reported to induce NO production in neuronal and endothelial cells as part of mechanotransduction pathways.
source: In older literature, LN was reported to induce NO production in neuronal and endothelial cells as part of mechanotransduction pathways (Gloe and Pohl, 2002; Rialas et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: NO is a potent activator of p53.
source: As NO is reported to be a potent activator of p53 (Forrester et al., 1996; Wang et al., 2002), we hypothesized that LNs might also be instrumental in inducing NO production in breast cells, which in turn would activate p53.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Application of purified LN5 to MCF10A cells increased pSer20-p53 after 30 min.
source: We applied purified LN5 (Figure 7a) or lrECM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a) to MCF10A cells and observed an increase in pSer20-p53 after 30 min, along with increases in Ser1981-phosphorylated ATM and total level of p14 ARF, the known p53 activators (Canman et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7a and citations to support the role of ATM and p14 ARF.

claim: Application of lrECM to MCF10A cells increased pSer20-p53 after 30 min.
source: We applied purified LN5 (Figure 7a) or lrECM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a) to MCF10A cells and observed an increase in pSer20-p53 after 30 min, along with increases in Ser1981-phosphorylated ATM and total level of p14 ARF, the known p53 activators (Canman et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7—figure supplement 1a and citations to support the role of ATM and p14 ARF.

claim: Application of purified LN5 or lrECM to MCF10A cells increased Ser1981-phosphorylated ATM and total level of p14 ARF after 30 min.
source: We applied purified LN5 (Figure 7a) or lrECM (Figure 7—figure supplement 1a) to MCF10A cells and observed an increase in pSer20-p53 after 30 min, along with increases in Ser1981-phosphorylated ATM and total level of p14 ARF, the known p53 activators (Canman et al., 1998; Zhang et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a, and citations to support the role of ATM and p14 ARF.

claim: Ser1417 phosphorylation of nitric oxide synthase 1 (NOS-1) was elevated after application of purified LN5 or lrECM to MCF10A cells.
source: Under the same conditions, Ser1417 phosphorylation of nitric oxide synthase 1 (NOS-1) was also elevated (Figure 7a, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a), suggesting its role in NO production.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: DNp53 overexpressed in MCF10A cells was not activated in response to laminins, whereas ATM, p14 ARF and NOS-1 were all activated.
source: In contrast, DNp53 overexpressed in MCF10A cells was not activated in response to LNs, whereas ATM, p14 ARF and NOS-1 were all activated (Figure 7a, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Treatment of MCF10A cells with L-NAME severely impaired LN5-mediated activation of p53, ATM and p14 ARF.
source: When MCF10A cells were treated with a NOS inhibitor, L-NAME, that inhibits NO production, LN5-mediated activation of p53, as well as of ATM and p14 ARF, were severely impaired (Figure 7b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7b.

claim: S1 and MCF10A cells produced NO in response to LN5 or lrECM.
source: S1 and MCF10A cells produced NO as a function of time in response to LN5 or lrECM (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7c and 7d.

claim: T4-2 cells failed to produce NO in response to LN5 or lrECM.
source: By contrast, T4-2 cells failed to do so (Figure 7c and d).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7c and 7d.

claim: Addition of collagen-1 (COL1) did not induce NO production by S1 or MCF10A cells.
source: Addition of another ECM protein collagen-1 (COL1) did not induce NO production by S1 or MCF10A cells (Figure 7e), suggesting a unique role of LNs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7e.

claim: NO level peaked at around 1 hr after lrECM addition and declined thereafter in S1 and MCF10A cells.
source: NO level peaked at around 1 hr after lrECM addition and declined thereafter in S1 and MCF10A cells, whereas it remained low in T4-2 cells (Figure 7f, Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7f and Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: NO level remained low in T4-2 cells after lrECM addition.
source: NO level peaked at around 1 hr after lrECM addition and declined thereafter in S1 and MCF10A cells, whereas it remained low in T4-2 cells (Figure 7f, Figure 7—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7f and Figure 7—figure supplement 1b.

claim: S1 acini showed strong basolateral SNOC staining.
source: S1 acini showed strong basolateral SNOC staining, whereas T4-2 cells showed weak and dispersed staining.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: T4-2 cells showed weak and dispersed SNOC staining.
source: S1 acini showed strong basolateral SNOC staining, whereas T4-2 cells showed weak and dispersed staining.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: T4-2 Rev cells restored the strong basolateral SNOC staining analogous to S1.
source: However, T4-2 Rev cells restored the strong basolateral SNOC staining analogous to S1, suggesting the recovery of NO production upon phenotypic reversion (Figure 7g, Figure 7—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7g and Figure 7—figure supplement 1c.

claim: Normal mammary epithelia were distinctively stained for SNOC, whereas the majority of tumor samples were only weakly and diffusely stained.
source: Normal mammary epithelia were distinctively stained for SNOC, whereas the majority of tumor samples were only weakly and diffusely stained [positive staining (intensity >+1): 8/8 vs. 8/32, respectively] (Figure 7h).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7h.

claim: NO plays a role in the differentiation and morphogenesis of neurons, muscles and immune cells.
source: NO is known to play a role in the differentiation and morphogenesis of neurons, muscles and immune cells (Rialas et al., 2000; Stamler and Meissner, 2001; Niedbala et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Inhibiting NO production with L-NAME in non-malignant breast epithelial cells led to the formation of disorganized proliferative structures in lrECM.
source: To test the involvement of NO in mammary morphogenesis, we inhibited NO production with L-NAME in two different non-malignant breast epithelial cells; this led to the formation of disorganized proliferative structures in lrECM (Figure 8a and b, Figure 8—figure supplement 1a and b).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 8a, 8b, Figure 8—figure supplement 1a and 1b.

claim: Induction of NO production in T4-2 cells with a NO donor, SNAP, induced phenotypic reversion.
source: Alternatively, the induction of NO production in T4-2 cells with a NO donor, SNAP, induced phenotypic reversion (Figure 8c, Figure 8—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 8c and Figure 8—figure supplement 1c.

claim: L-NAME treatment dramatically reduced the percentage of breast organoid colonies capable of alveologenesis in ex vivo 3D cultures.
source: L-NAME treatment dramatically reduced the percentage of colonies capable of alveologenesis (vehicle-treated: 28% vs. L-NAME-treated: 1.2%) (Figure 8d, Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 8d and Videos 1 and 2.

claim: Acinar forming non-malignant breast cells undergo coherent angular motion (CAMo) in lrECM, whereas cancer cells exhibit random amoeboid motion.
source: We and others have shown previously that acinar forming non-malignant breast cells undergo CAMo in lrECM, whereas cancer cells exhibit random amoeboid motion (Tanner et al., 2012; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous work by the authors and others, with citations to support the claim.

claim: S1 cells treated with L-NAME are defective in CAMo and form disorganized masses.
source: S1 cells treated with L-NAME are defective in CAMo and form disorganized masses (Figure 8e, Videos 3 and 4).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 8e and Videos 3 and 4.

claim: NO production in response to lrECM is critical for p53 activation and the formation of mammary acini.
source: We showed above that NO production in response to lrECM is critical for p53 activation and the formation of mammary acini (Figures 7a–g and 8a–e).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The process of acinar formation involves de novo synthesized LN5.
source: This process involves de novo synthesized LN5 (Figure 6a and b).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with reference to Figure 6a and 6b.

claim: p53 upregulates the expression of HOXD10 and downregulates activation of NFκB.
source: We also showed that p53 upregulates the expression of HOXD10 and downregulates activation of NFκB.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The dual action of p53 allows expression of the three miRNAs that inhibit TFs, SCAI and EIF5A2, to downmodulate MMP-9 expression.
source: This dual action allows expression of the three miRNAs that inhibit TFs, SCAI and EIF5A2, to downmodulate MMP-9 expression.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of MMP-9 expression leads to inhibition of laminin protein degradation, leading to the closure of the morphogenetic loop.
source: The result is inhibition of laminin protein degradation, leading to the closure of the morphogenetic loop (Figure 9a).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with reference to Figure 9a.

claim: The promoter region of the LAMA3 gene contained the CpG island that harbors numerous p53-binding sites around the transcription start site.
source: PROMO analysis of the promoter of LAMA3 chain of LN5 revealed over 20 high-confidence p53 binding sites within 1 kb length of the CpG island around the transcription start site (% dissimilarity <8%; genomic frequency <1×10−3) (Figure 9b, Table 8) (Farré et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 9b and Table 8, and a citation to the PROMO database.

claim: LAMA3 expression in S1 cells could be abrogated by p53 inhibition with α-pifithrin.
source: Consistently, LAMA3 expression in S1 cells, could be abrogated by p53 inhibition with α-pifithrin (Figure 9c, Figure 9—figure supplement 1a), whereas ectopic addition of LN5 or lrECM, elevated LAMA3 transcription (Figure 9d, Figure 9—figure supplement 1b) in parallel to the activation of wild-type p53 (Figure 7a, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 9c and Figure 9—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Ectopic addition of LN5 or lrECM elevated LAMA3 transcription in parallel to the activation of wild-type p53.
source: Consistently, LAMA3 expression in S1 cells, could be abrogated by p53 inhibition with α-pifithrin (Figure 9c, Figure 9—figure supplement 1a), whereas ectopic addition of LN5 or lrECM, elevated LAMA3 transcription (Figure 9d, Figure 9—figure supplement 1b) in parallel to the activation of wild-type p53 (Figure 7a, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 9d, Figure 9—figure supplement 1b, Figure 7a, and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a.

claim: All normal breast tissue sections were stained strongly with antibodies against wild-type p53 and LAMA3.
source: All normal breast tissue sections were stained strongly with both antibodies (Figure 9—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 9—figure supplement 1c.

claim: The reciprocity between LN5 and wild-type p53 remains strong even as cells progress to malignancy, with the levels of the two proteins falling in parallel in tumor samples.
source: The reciprocity between LN5 and wild-type p53 remains strong even as cells progress to malignancy. The levels of the two proteins fell in parallel in the tumor samples (R = 0.51, p<0.0001, n = 117) (Figure 9e).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 9e.

claim: The ability to phenotypically revert breast cancer cells by inhibiting a single signaling pathway in 3D lrECM has provided the means to identify additional major signaling pathways that must integrate for the formation of 'phenotypically normal' human breast acini.
source: The ability to phenotypically revert breast cancer cells by inhibiting a single signaling pathway in 3D lrECM has provided us with the means to identify additional major signaling pathways that must integrate for the formation of 'phenotypically normal' human breast acini (Weaver et al., 1997; Muschler et al., 2002; Beliveau et al., 2010; Bissell and Hines, 2011; Lee et al., 2012; Tanner et al., 2012; Becker-Weimann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Although T4-2 Rev cells have similar phenotypes, their gene expression patterns were very different.
source: We observed that, although T4-2 Rev cells have similar phenotypes, their gene expression patterns were very different (Becker-Weimann et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Diverse biological activities in development are regulated by tissue–tissue and tissue–microenvironment interactions and signaling.
source: It has been long known that diverse biological activities in development are regulated by tissue–tissue and tissue–microenvironment interactions and signaling (Wessells, 1977; Chiquet-Ehrismann et al., 1986; Howlett and Bissell, 1993; Hogan, 1999; Bhat and Bissell, 2014).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: During development, different cell types communicate and coordinate with each other through negative and positive feedback regulations.
source: During development, different cell types communicate and coordinate with each other through negative and positive feedback regulations.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Tissue formation starts with cells moving within a soft microenvironment such as lrECM, as observed for mammary acini; this movement is termed 'coherent angular motion'.
source: In addition, similar to movements that are being discovered in the formation of embryos during development (Haigo and Bilder, 2011), tissue formation starts with cells moving within a soft microenvironment such as lrECM, as we and others observed for mammary acini; we termed this 'coherent angular motion' (Tanner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors and others, with citations to support the claim.

claim: CAMo creates polarity and adhesion by interacting with exogenous ECM to lay down its own endogenous tissue-specific ECM.
source: CAMo creates polarity and adhesion by interacting with exogenous ECM to lay down its own endogenous tissue-specific ECM (Tanner et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The balance and integration of the different signaling pathways and dynamic interactions between epithelial cells and the ECM drive the remodeling of the ECM, including formation of the BM that helps to anchor the epithelia.
source: The balance and integration of the different signaling pathways and dynamic interactions between epithelial cells and the ECM drive the remodeling of the ECM, including formation of the BM that helps to anchor the epithelia (Weaver et al., 2002) and that protects the cells within the tissues from apoptosis.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Changes in the ECM regulate cell proliferation, survival, migration, shape and adhesion, ultimately sculpting and maintaining tissue architecture.
source: Such changes in the ECM regulate cell proliferation, survival, migration, shape and adhesion, ultimately sculpting and maintaining tissue architecture (Wessells, 1977; Chiquet-Ehrismann et al., 1986; Howlett and Bissell, 1993; Hogan, 1999; Bhat and Bissell, 2014; Haigo and Bilder, 2011; Weaver et al., 2002; Daley and Yamada, 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Unlike the signaling pathways in development, the stability of the differentiated state does not appear to be hierarchical.
source: Unlike the signaling pathways in development, the stability of the differentiated state does not appear to be hierarchical.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The stability of the differentiated state reflects the balance between growth and differentiation, between the negative and positive signaling pathways, and between the formation of a BM and the destruction of ECM by degrading enzymes.
source: Instead, it reflects the balance between growth and differentiation, between the negative and positive signaling pathways, and between the formation of a BM and the destruction of ECM by degrading enzymes that determines the stability of the differentiated state in the tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: NO is a pivotal player in reciprocal cell–ECM interactions in breast morphogenesis.
source: Another novel finding here is that NO is a pivotal player in reciprocal cell–ECM interactions in breast morphogenesis, but tumor cells produce only a small amount of NO unless the architecture is re-established and the cells have reverted to a 'dormant state' (Figure 7c–e and g).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with reference to Figure 7c-e and 7g.

claim: Tumor cells produce only a small amount of NO unless the architecture is re-established and the cells have reverted to a 'dormant state'.
source: Another novel finding here is that NO is a pivotal player in reciprocal cell–ECM interactions in breast morphogenesis, but tumor cells produce only a small amount of NO unless the architecture is re-established and the cells have reverted to a 'dormant state' (Figure 7c–e and g).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with reference to Figure 7c-e and 7g.

claim: NO production is a mechanistic link between proper architecture and proper function in breast tissues.
source: These findings demonstrate that NO production is a mechanistic link between proper architecture and proper function in breast tissues.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: The levels of NO produced endogenously in response to LNs in this study are at least 500-fold lower than those used in the literature.
source: It is crucial to note that the levels of NO produced endogenously in response to LNs in our studies, as well as the exogenous NO levels required for the reciprocal loop we describe here, are at least 500-fold lower than those used in the literature (Forrester et al., 1996; Gloe et al., 1999; Gordon et al., 2001).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with citations to support the comparison.

claim: Increased levels of NO are produced by the mammary gland of postpartum mammals.
source: NO has been reported to play an important role during lactation. Increased levels of NO are produced by the mammary gland of postpartum mammals (Akçay et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: NO promotes blood flow and the nutrient uptake of mammary glands for milk production.
source: NO promotes blood flow and the nutrient uptake of mammary glands for milk production (Kim and Wu, 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: NO is proposed to facilitate milk ejection by inducing contraction of myoepithelial cells in mammary glands as well as smooth muscle cells in the stroma.
source: NO is also proposed to facilitate milk ejection by inducing contraction of myoepithelial cells (MEPs) in mammary glands as well as smooth muscle cells in the stroma (Iizuka et al., 1998; Adriance et al., 2005; Tezer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: NO is secreted into the breast milk as an essential component for immunity in neonatal growth.
source: In addition, NO is secreted into the breast milk as an essential component for immunity in neonatal growth (Hord et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: NO plays additional and significant roles in breast morphogenesis.
source: Using 3D cultures and ex vivo cultures of human mammary glands, we showed here that NO also plays additional and significant roles in breast morphogenesis (Figure 8a, b and d).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with reference to Figure 8a, 8b and 8d.

claim: NO production was specific to LNs and was not induced by collagen.
source: Importantly, NO production was specific to LNs and was not induced by collagen (Figure 7c-e).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7c-e.

claim: LNs and COL1 elicit opposite actions on epithelia.
source: We and others had shown previously that LNs and COL1 elicit opposite actions on epithelia (Gudjonsson et al., 2002; Oktay et al., 2000; Chamoux et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from previous work by the authors and others, with citations to support the claim.

claim: LNs activate NOS-1.
source: We showed here that LNs activate NOS-1 (Figure 7a, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a), supporting previous observations by others that NOS-1 is expressed in the mammary tissue at appreciable levels — in particular in MEPs during pregnancy and lactation in humans (Tezer et al., 2012) and rodents (Iizuka et al., 1998; Islam et al., 2009; Wockel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study, with reference to Figure 7a and Figure 7—figure supplement 1a, and citations to support the expression of NOS-1.

claim: NOS-1 is expressed in the mammary tissue at appreciable levels — in particular in MEPs during pregnancy and lactation in humans and rodents.
source: We showed here that LNs activate NOS-1 (Figure 7a, Figure 7—figure supplement 1a), supporting previous observations by others that NOS-1 is expressed in the mammary tissue at appreciable levels — in particular in MEPs during pregnancy and lactation in humans (Tezer et al., 2012) and rodents (Iizuka et al., 1998; Islam et al., 2009; Wockel et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Dystroglycan (DG) is speculated to be the molecule responsible for linking LNs to NOS-1.
source: As the molecule that appears to be responsible for linking LNs to NOS-1, we speculate the involvement of the LN receptor, dystroglycan (DG), which is known to form a multi-protein complex involving LNs and NOS-1, in mediating the mechanotransduction of muscle cells (Rando, 2001; Garbincius and Michele, 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a speculation based on established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: DG plays a critical signaling role in breast epithelial cells.
source: We had shown previously that DG also plays a critical signaling role in breast epithelial cells (Muschler et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous work by the authors, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: DG anchors the BM protein, in particular LNs, to the cell surface, allowing for LN polymerization and transduction of signals for the formation of polarized colonies.
source: DG anchors the BM protein, in particular LNs, to the cell surface, allowing for LN polymerization and transduction of signals for the formation of polarized colonies (Weir et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: DG–LN interaction is impaired in different types of cancer cells and correlates with poorer patient prognosis.
source: Such DG–LN interaction is impaired in different types of cancer cells and correlates with poorer patient prognosis (Akhavan et al., 2012; Esser et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Form and function are maintained in adult organs throughout most of the life of the organism, despite constant mutations and damage from environmental assaults and aging.
source: Form and function are maintained in adult organs throughout most of the life of the organism, despite constant mutations and damage from environmental assaults and aging.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: To maintain the correct tissue function throughout the lifetime of the organisms, signaling pathways have to integrate in order to prevent chaos and malfunction.
source: To maintain the correct tissue function throughout the lifetime of the organisms, signaling pathways have to integrate in order to prevent chaos and malfunction.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Evolution has packed much wisdom and specificity onto the ECM, which appears to instruct the chromatin to change shape and thus also gene expression.
source: Evolution has packed much wisdom and specificity onto the ECM, which appears to instruct the chromatin to change shape and thus also gene expression, as seen in Figure 4e.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with reference to Figure 4e.

claim: When cells on flat surfaces receive LNs, not only their shape, but also many of their signaling pathways are altered.
source: When cells on flat surfaces receive LNs, not only their shape, but also many of their signaling pathways are altered (Figure 1) (Bissell et al., 2005); growth must stop in many tissues (Spencer et al., 2011; Fiore et al., 2017) and differentiation and cell death must be coordinated.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with reference to Figure 1 and citations to support the claim.

claim: Growth must stop in many tissues when cells receive LNs.
source: When cells on flat surfaces receive LNs, not only their shape, but also many of their signaling pathways are altered (Figure 1) (Bissell et al., 2005); growth must stop in many tissues (Spencer et al., 2011; Fiore et al., 2017) and differentiation and cell death must be coordinated.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from the literature, with citations to support the claim.

claim: Narratives that are based solely on linear and irreversible regulatory dynamics cannot satisfactorily explain the reality in vivo.
source: It is now clear that narratives that are based solely on linear and irreversible regulatory dynamics cannot satisfactorily explain the reality in vivo (Hogan, 1999).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with a citation to support the claim.

claim: At the last analysis, it is the 3D architecture of the tissue itself that is the message.
source: It is also clear that, at the last analysis, it is the 3D architecture of the tissue itself that is the message (Hagios et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in the manuscript, with a citation to support the claim.
